passage:
Subject: sorry about yesterday
Sumit,
I know I yelled at you in the canteen. You only asked if I'd done the chemistry assignment and I told you to mind your own business in front of everyone. I haven't done it. I haven't done anything since Ma died. I come home, shut my door and lie there. Papa knocks and I say I'm studying.
The thing is, I'm not even angry at you. I'm angry that the doctors couldn't fix it, that Papa couldn't, that everyone keeps saying 'be strong' like it's a switch. Mostly I'm scared. Of what happens to us now. Of forgetting her voice.
Don't tell anyone. But don't give up on me either.
Mridul

qa.q: What had Sumit asked Mridul in the canteen?
qa.a: He only asked if Mridul had done the chemistry assignment.

qa.q: What feelings does Mridul reveal beneath his anger?
qa.a: Fear about what happens to his family now and of forgetting his mother's voice, along with helplessness that no one could fix it.

qa.q: What could help Mridul at this stage besides Sumit's friendship?
qa.a: Talking to a trusted adult, like his Papa or the school counsellor, so he isn't carrying the fear alone behind a closed door.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel reading this email?
qa.a: Probably relieved the anger wasn't really about him, and worried for Mridul, wanting to stay close while hoping he gets more support.

grounding: A teenager who lost his mother snaps at a friend, skips work and shuts his door, and admits fear and helplessness beneath the anger.

passage: You want to know why I've been such a monster, Gautam? Fine. Since Papa died in March, everything makes me furious. Kirti laughs too loud at lunch and I want to throw my tray. The class teacher says 'take your time with the syllabus' and I want to scream that time is exactly what we didn't have. I skipped two tests. I stay in my room with the door locked and headphones on, even when Ma knocks and says, 'Jaya, eat something.' Everyone says he's in a better place. Better than here? With us? I'm angry at the doctors, at everything, at the grown-ups who kept saying it'd be okay. And under all that... I'm scared. Of Ma crying at night. Of it happening again. There. Happy now?

qa.q: How many tests has Jaya skipped?
qa.a: She skipped two tests.

qa.q: What is Jaya really feeling beneath the fury?
qa.a: She's scared, of her mother crying at night and of losing someone again, and helpless because the adults couldn't keep their promise that it would be okay.

qa.q: What could Gautam do after hearing this?
qa.a: Stay with her without arguing, and gently encourage her to talk to her Ma or a school counsellor so she isn't alone with the fear.

qa.q: What might Jaya's Ma be going through when she knocks on the locked door?
qa.a: She is grieving too and probably worried and lonely, wanting to reach her daughter but not knowing how.

grounding: A teenage girl who lost her father snaps at friends, skips tests and locks her door, with fear and helplessness beneath her anger.

passage:
In the village near Ujjain, Vaibhav hadn't been to the tuition class since his father's death two months ago. When his friend Ritesh came by with notes, Vaibhav snapped, "Who asked you?" and shut the door of his room.
His mother, Indu, heard the bolt slide. She knocked softly. "Vaibhav?"
"Leave me alone!"
Inside, he sat on the floor with his back against the bed. He wasn't really angry at Ritesh. He was angry at the hospital, at the doctors, at the whole unfair world. And underneath, he was scared. If Papa could just be gone, what else could?
Indu sat down outside his door, her back against it too, and waited.

qa.q: How long ago did Vaibhav's father die?
qa.a: Two months ago.

qa.q: What feelings sat underneath Vaibhav's anger?
qa.a: Fear and helplessness; he felt the world was unfair and was scared that anything could be taken away.

qa.q: What turning point does Indu's choice to sit by the door offer?
qa.a: It shows she is there without forcing him, so when he is ready, he can talk or let her in.

qa.q: How might Ritesh feel after being snapped at?
qa.a: Ritesh may feel hurt and unsure, but could understand it isn't really about him.

grounding: Shows a teen who lost his father snapping at a friend and shutting himself in, with fear and helplessness beneath the anger.

passage:
In Oslo it was already dark at three. Rosa hadn't been to school for four days. Her mother had died in the spring, and now, in November, Rosa was angrier than ever.
When Ulla knocked with a bag of cinnamon buns, Rosa opened the door a crack. "I don't need your pity."
"It's not pity. It's buns."
"Just go, Ulla."
She shut the door and leaned on it. She could hear Ulla still standing there. Rosa pressed her fists against her eyes. Why were the adults useless? Why couldn't the hospital have done something? It wasn't fair.
After a minute she opened the door again. Ulla was still there. Rosa took the bag without a word.

qa.q: What did Ulla bring?
qa.a: A bag of cinnamon buns.

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling as she leaned on the door?
qa.a: She felt angry and helpless, furious that adults and the hospital couldn't save her mother and that life is unfair.

qa.q: What small turning point happened when Rosa opened the door again?
qa.a: Taking the bag let a little connection back in, even without words.

qa.q: What is it like for Ulla to be told to go?
qa.a: Ulla probably feels hurt but understanding, choosing to stay by the door because she cares.

grounding: Shows a grieving teen snapping at a friend and shutting her door, her anger covering helplessness and a sense of unfairness.

passage:
The school counsellor's room was small, with one plant and two chairs. Sunaina sat with her arms folded.
"Your teachers say you've stopped handing in work," Seema ma'am said gently. "And that you shouted at your friends in the canteen."
"So?"
"It's been three months since your father died."
"What's that got to do with anything?" Sunaina's voice cracked on the last word. "Everyone keeps saying it'll get better. The doctors said he'd get better too."
Seema ma'am waited.
"Nobody could fix it," Sunaina whispered. "Not even the adults." She put her face in her hands.
"No," Seema ma'am said. "Nobody could. I'm here, and we'll meet every week."

qa.q: How long ago did Sunaina's father die?
qa.a: Three months ago.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's cracking voice suggest about her anger?
qa.a: Underneath the anger she feels helpless and betrayed, since even the adults and doctors could not fix it.

qa.q: What support does Seema ma'am offer at this stage?
qa.a: Honest words that nobody could fix it, her calm presence, and a regular weekly meeting.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's friends see her shouting in the canteen?
qa.a: They may feel hurt and confused, not knowing her anger comes from grief about her father.

grounding: Shows a grieving teen who snaps at friends and stops working, with helplessness and unfairness beneath the anger, and a counsellor's steady support.

passage:
Imran,
I'm writing this because I can't say it out loud without getting angry again. Sorry for yelling at you at the nets on Friday. You only asked if I was coming to practice, and I told you to mind your own business, in front of everyone.
Since Appa died in March I've been like this. I slam my door. I haven't opened my physics book in three weeks. Amma knocks and I say "leave me," and then I feel horrible. Everyone keeps telling me to be strong. The doctors couldn't fix him, the adults couldn't fix anything, so what is the point of strong?
I don't think I'm really angry at you. I think I'm scared all the time. Of Amma being alone. Of forgetting his voice.
The school counsellor asked me to come on Monday. I said yes. Will you walk there with me?
Lokesh

qa.q: When did Lokesh yell at Imran?
qa.a: At the nets on Friday, in front of everyone.

qa.q: What feelings does Lokesh say sit beneath the anger?
qa.a: Lokesh feels scared all the time: afraid of Amma being alone and of forgetting Appa's voice.

qa.q: What step has Lokesh already taken, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Lokesh agreed to see the school counsellor on Monday, which brings a trusted adult in to help with the grief.

qa.q: How might Imran feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Imran may feel relieved and moved, understanding the yelling came from grief and fear, not from anything Imran did.

grounding: Shows a bereaved teenager snapping at friends, skipping study and shutting the door, with fear and helplessness beneath the anger.
